# OneCoin / Cryptoqueen Network: Investigative Report

## Executive assessment

The evidence provided supports the conclusion that OneCoin was an international investment-fraud scheme presented as a cryptocurrency and distributed through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) structure. The publicly documented principal founders were Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood. According to the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), the pair and others orchestrated the scheme from 2014 through 2019, while the related legal commentary describes Greenwood as OneCoin’s leading MLM distributor and a major beneficiary of the network. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The evidence also supports a distinction between the enforcement record and unresolved claims concerning Ignatova. Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison and was ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000, according to the provided legal analysis. The DOJ separately states that more than $40 million in forfeited assets is available for victim compensation. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison); [U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

By contrast, the evidence does not establish what happened to Ignatova after she became a fugitive. The DOJ describes her as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive and asks the public to submit information concerning her whereabouts. That establishes an official fugitive status and an active law-enforcement interest, but it does not prove that she is alive, dead, in hiding, or located in any particular country. Any stronger conclusion would exceed the supplied evidence. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

Two sources were supplied:

| Source ID | Source | Date | Evidentiary character |
|---|---|---:|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of Justice, “Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture” | April 13, 2026 | Primary government source concerning the scheme, prosecutions, forfeiture, victim compensation, and Ignatova’s official fugitive status |
| S2 | ArentFox Schiff, “Co-Founder of Fraudulent Cryptocurrency Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison” | September 15, 2023 | Secondary legal analysis summarizing the Greenwood prosecution, sentence, alleged conduct, and financial figures |

S1 is the more authoritative source for current enforcement and victim-remission information because it is an official DOJ announcement. S2 is useful for additional detail regarding Greenwood’s role, the claimed number of investors, the alleged misrepresentations, and the sentence, but it should be treated as a secondary summary of government allegations and enforcement outcomes. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

## Reconstruction of the OneCoin scheme

### Formation and geographic base

The DOJ states that OneCoin Ltd. began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. It marketed and sold a cryptocurrency called OneCoin through a global MLM network. The DOJ identifies Ignatova and Greenwood as co-founders and states that they, together with others, orchestrated the investment scheme between 2014 and 2019. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The secondary source adds that OneCoin began operating in the United States around 2015. The supplied material does not provide a precise date for the U.S. launch, identify specific U.S. offices, or describe the corporate chain of entities beyond OneCoin Ltd. Accordingly, the supported conclusion is limited to the existence of Bulgarian operations beginning in 2014 and a U.S. presence beginning approximately in 2015. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

### Cryptocurrency presentation and alleged deception

The evidence describes OneCoin as a fraudulent cryptocurrency rather than a functioning digital asset supported by the characteristics claimed in its marketing. According to the legal analysis, prosecutors alleged that OneCoin represented its value as being determined by market supply and demand, while the value was actually set arbitrarily without regard to market forces. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

Prosecutors also alleged that Greenwood claimed OneCoin had a private blockchain capable of identifying OneCoins and recording historical transactions, even though no publicly verifiable blockchain existed. This allegation is significant because it concerns the technical foundation and verifiability of the product being sold. The supplied evidence does not independently establish the technical architecture of OneCoin; it establishes that these representations were part of the government’s case as summarized by S2. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The DOJ characterizes the conduct more broadly as misrepresentations made in connection with the sale of OneCoin. It states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide. S2 reports that the government charged Greenwood and others with obtaining more than $4 billion from approximately 3.5 million investors. The difference in wording should be preserved: S1 provides the official figure of more than $4 billion in worldwide victim investment, while S2 adds the approximate investor count. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

### MLM distribution structure

The scheme’s distribution model was a global MLM network. OneCoin members were allegedly paid commissions for recruiting others to purchase cryptocurrency packages. This structure made recruitment an important mechanism for expanding the investor base and distributing the product. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The evidence identifies Greenwood as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor. S2 states that he allegedly earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling more than $300 million. The use of “allegedly” is important because the supplied source presents the amount as a government allegation or prosecutorial account rather than as an independently documented accounting finding in the material provided. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The available record therefore supports a role distinction:

| Individual | Supported role | Qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Ruja Ignatova | Co-founder of OneCoin; identified by DOJ as one of the people who orchestrated the scheme | The supplied evidence does not provide a detailed division of operational responsibilities |
| Karl Sebastian Greenwood | Co-founder; top MLM distributor; alleged recipient of 5% of monthly OneCoin sales | The $300 million figure is presented as an allegation in the secondary source |
| Other participants | Participants in the broader scheme and related prosecutions | The supplied material does not identify all such individuals or assign them specific roles |

## Principal founders and enforcement outcomes

### Ruja Ignatova

The DOJ identifies Ignatova as a co-founder of OneCoin and as one of the individuals who orchestrated the scheme. The supplied material does not state that she has been arrested, tried, convicted, sentenced, or located. It states instead that she remains at large and is an FBI Top Ten Fugitive. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The DOJ asks anyone with information concerning Ignatova to submit it through the FBI’s tip system or telephone tipline. This indicates continuing investigative activity. It does not, however, establish the factual truth of any particular theory concerning her disappearance or current condition. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

Greenwood is identified in both sources as a co-founder. S2 states that he is a citizen of Sweden and the United Kingdom and that he was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his alleged role in the $4 billion fraud scheme. The same source states that he was ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. ([ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The DOJ confirms that several key figures connected with OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York have been sentenced, although the provided DOJ text does not separately restate Greenwood’s sentence or provide a complete sentencing chronology. S2 supplies the specific 20-year sentence. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

### Investigative and prosecutorial agencies

The DOJ states that the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation conducted the criminal fraud investigation. It also identifies significant assistance from the DOJ Office of International Affairs and states that the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the remission process. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The Southern District of New York brought several OneCoin-related prosecutions. The supplied evidence does not enumerate every defendant, charge, trial result, or sentence. It therefore supports an agency-level reconstruction but not a complete network chart. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

## Asset forfeiture and victim compensation

The DOJ announced that more than $40 million in forfeited assets was available for victim compensation through a remission process. Victims who purchased OneCoin between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible. The announcement states that petitions could be obtained through the designated remission website or from the remission administrator, with a filing deadline of June 30; the supplied text does not expressly state the year attached to that deadline. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

Kroll Settlement Administration LLC was identified as the remission administrator. The DOJ also states that the process is managed by the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section and that the Asset Forfeiture Program has returned more than $12.5 billion in forfeited assets to crime victims since 2000. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The DOJ expressly warned that neither the remission administrator nor the Department would ask victims to pay to participate. This warning is relevant because fraud victims may be targeted by impersonators or purported recovery services. The supplied DOJ announcement directs victims toward the official remission process and cautions against individuals or organizations claiming to represent the government or administrator without an established prior connection. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

## Enforcement facts versus unresolved claims

| Issue | Supported enforcement fact | Unresolved or unsupported point |
|---|---|---|
| Nature of OneCoin | DOJ and prosecutors characterized it as a fraudulent cryptocurrency investment scheme | The supplied materials do not provide an independent technical audit |
| Founders | Ignatova and Greenwood are identified as co-founders | The materials do not specify every founder-level operational responsibility |
| Greenwood | Sentenced to 20 years; approximately $300,000 forfeiture reported by S2 | The supplied materials do not provide the full judgment or sentencing memorandum |
| Ignatova | Identified as a co-founder, alleged orchestrator, and FBI Top Ten Fugitive who remains at large | No supplied evidence resolves her location, condition, or ultimate fate |
| Victim losses | More than $4 billion worldwide; approximately 3.5 million investors reported by S2 | The supplied materials do not provide a complete victim ledger |
| Recovery | More than $40 million in forfeited assets available for compensation | The materials do not state the final amount each eligible victim will receive |
| Network scope | Global MLM network and multiple DOJ prosecutions | The supplied materials do not identify every participant or jurisdiction |

The central analytical judgment is therefore clear: the enforcement record sufficiently supports describing OneCoin as a large, internationally distributed fraud scheme involving deceptive cryptocurrency representations and MLM recruitment. It does not support converting allegations about Ignatova’s current status into established fact. The only defensible statement from the supplied evidence is that she is officially regarded as a fugitive and remains sought by U.S. authorities. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

## Contradictions and qualifications

There is no material factual contradiction between S1 and S2 concerning the central reconstruction. Both identify Ignatova and Greenwood as co-founders and describe OneCoin as a fraudulent cryptocurrency scheme. The apparent difference between Greenwood’s approximately $300,000 forfeiture and the more than $40 million available for victim compensation is not a contradiction: the first concerns a specific forfeiture order reported for Greenwood, while the second concerns the broader pool of forfeited assets available through the remission process. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

## Conclusion

The supplied evidence documents OneCoin as a global fraud network built around the sale of a purported cryptocurrency and expanded through MLM recruitment. Ignatova and Greenwood were its principal identified founders. Greenwood’s documented role included leadership in the MLM distribution system, and he received a 20-year prison sentence. Ignatova’s role is described as co-founder and alleged orchestrator, but her post-disappearance status remains unresolved except for the official designation that she is an FBI Top Ten Fugitive who remains at large. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [ArentFox Schiff, 2023](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The DOJ’s remission process is a concrete enforcement consequence of the case: more than $40 million in forfeited assets was identified for potential victim compensation. That recovery effort confirms that authorities pursued criminal forfeiture as well as prosecution, but the supplied evidence does not establish the ultimate recovery rate, distribution amount, or final number of compensated victims. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

## References

[https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs. (2026, April 13). *Justice Department announces compensation process for OneCoin fraud victims with funds recovered through asset forfeiture*. U.S. Department of Justice. [https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ Our Offices Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov Office of Public Affairs News Press Releases Justice Department Announces Compensation Process For OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture MENU News All News Blogs Photo Galleries Podcasts Press Releases Speeches Videos Archived Press Releases Archived News Press Release Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture Monday, April 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Today, the Department of Justice announced the beginning of the remission compensation process to provide recovery for victims of the international investment scheme involving OneCoin Ltd. Between 2014 and 2019, Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood, co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. (OneCoin), and others orchestrated a large, international cryptocurrency investment scheme defrauding investors from around the globe. OneCoin, which began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, marketed and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency by the same name through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. As a result of misrepresentations made about OneCoin, victims invested over $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency. The Department of Justice filed a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. Several key figures involved in the scheme have been sentenced, and the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the proceeds of the fraud scheme. More than $40 million in forfeited assets are currently available for victim compensation. Through the remission process, victims who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible for compensation. Individuals who believe they may be victims may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com . Victims may also call, email, or write to the Remission Administrator to request that a Petition Form be sent to them. The deadline for filing a petition is June 30. The Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the remission compensation process. “Victims are at the core of everything we do at the Department of Justice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. “As we did in this complex investment fraud case, the Department pursues forfeiture to take the profit out of crime and then use that money to compensate victims wherever possible. I commend the efforts of our colleagues in the Southern District of New York, our law enforcement partners, and our Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, which manages the Asset Forfeiture Program, for all of their work on behalf of the victims in this important case.” “Between 2014 and 2019, OneCoin’s founders sold a lie disguised as cryptocurrency, costing victims more than $4 billion worldwide,” said U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton for the Southern District of New York. “Today’s announcement marks an important step toward returning funds to those harmed. While no recovery can fully undo the damage, our Office will continue working to seize criminal proceeds and prioritize getting money back into the hands of victims. If you believe you may be a victim of OneCoin, you may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com.” “The victim losses accrued in this case are monumental,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr of the FBI New York Field Office. “Misled by falsified statements and empty promises, many unknowingly depleted their savings for a fraudulent investment scheme in an emerging financial ecosystem that would never pay out. With the unwavering support from the Department of Justice, the FBI maintains its commitment to returning these stolen funds to their rightful owners. Our office will continue its investigative pursuit of these criminal fraudsters — especially locating Ruja Ignatova, an FBI Top Ten Fugitive — alongside our partners at the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) and the Southern District of New York. Any information concerning this fugitive can be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov or via our tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI.” “The victims of the OneCoin scheme were misled and financially devastated by promises that were never real,” said Special Agent in Charge Jenifer L. Piovesan of IRS-CI. “Alongside our law enforcement partners, we worked tirelessly to trace illicit funds and recover them for victims. This compensation process represents a critical step toward returning stolen assets to those who were deceived. IRS-CI remains steadfast in its mission to follow the money and dismantle complex financial fraud schemes like OneCoin.” More information regarding the remission process, including eligibility criteria, updates, and frequently asked questions are available at www.onecoinremission.com or by calling 1-833-421-9748. Kroll Settlement Administration LLC is serving as the remission administrator in this matter. The FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs (OIA) provided significant assistance. The Department of Justice, through the Asset Forfeiture Program, works diligently to compensate victims of crime. Since 2000, the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), which oversees the Asset Forfeiture Program’s victim compensation program, has returned more than $12.5 billion in forfeited assets to victims of crime. MNF Attorney Advisor Drew Halter with the section’s Program Management and Training Unit is leading the remission process. Neither the Remission Administrator nor the Department of Justice will ask for any payment to participate in this remission process. Please be cautious of any individual or organization claiming to represent the Remission Administrator or the federal government in this matter. If you are a victim, any communications will come directly from the Remission Administrator or from government representatives with whom you have already had contact. How can we help you? Breadcrumb Insights Investigations Blog Co-Founder of Fraudulent Cryptocurrency Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison September 15, 2023 D. Jacques Smith , Randall A. Brater , Nadia Patel , Michael F. Dearington Share This Page Email LinkedIn X Facebook Headlines that Matter for Companies and Executives in Regulated Industries Off Co-Founder of Fraudulent Cryptocurrency Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison Karl Sebastian Greenwood, a citizen of Sweden and the United Kingdom and co-founder of the cryptocurrency OneCoin, was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his alleged role in a $4 billion fraud scheme. As described by prosecutors, OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency with the same name through a multi-level-marketing (MLM) scheme. Around 2015, OneCoin began operating in the United States. The government charged Greenwood and others with making various misrepresentations about OneCoin to secure over $4 billion in investments from approximately 3.5 million investors. These alleged misrepresentations include claiming that OneCoin’s value was based on market supply and demand though the value was actually set arbitrarily without regard to market forces. Greenwood also claimed to have a private blockchain to identify OneCoins and record historical transactions, when no public verifiable blockchain actually existed. According to the government, OneCoin marketed its cryptocurrency through a global MLM network whereby OneCoin members would receive commissions for recruiting others to purchase cryptocurrency packages. As OneCoin’s top MLM distributor, Greenwood is alleged to have earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling over $300 million. In addition to his 20-year prison term, Greenwood was ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. OneCoin’s other co-founder, Ruja Ignatova, remains at large and was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. A link to the US Department of Justice’s (DOJ) press release can be found here. Prison Inmate Pleads Guilty in COVID-19 Relief Fraud Telvin Breaux, an inmate in a California prison, and three other co-defendants pleaded guilty to conspiracy and aggravated identity theft charges for their alleged roles in a $25 million unemployment benefits scheme. According to the DOJ, Breaux and his co-defendants obtained personal identifying information of other inmates, as well as patients and customers at hospitals, dentists’ offices, and other businesses where one of the co-defendants worked or had connections. Breaux and his co-defendants then used this information to submit fraudulent unemployment insurance claims to the California Employment Development Department (EDD). In connection with these false claims, Breaux and his co-defendants also made specific misrepresentations that the individuals whose information they stole were unable to work as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. In total, defendants are alleged to have submitted over 400 fraudulent claims totaling over $25 million to the EDD, $5.4 million of which was actually paid out and used by the defendants to purchase luxury vehicles, fund trips to Las Vegas, and pay rent and tuition. Each defendant faces a maximum of 22 years imprisonment as well as fines of $250,000. A link to the DOJ’s press release can be found here. Former NYC Non-Profit Finance Director Sentenced to 18 Months Imprisonment Donna Murray, the former finance director of a New York City-based nonprofit financial services trade association with over 600 members, was sentenced to 18 months imprisonment for allegedly embezzling nearly half a million dollars from the nonprofit. The government alleges that Murray was the nonprofit’s sole finance department employee and was responsible for maintaining the organization’s books and records, handling accounts receivable and payable, and managing financial statements to outside auditors. In addition, Murray is alleged to have been the only employee with the ability to make wire transfers for the organization. As detailed in the DOJ’s information, Murray was charged with a months-long embezzlement scheme in which she stole over $488,000 from the organization’s bank accounts through 105 unauthorized wire transfers to her personal account. Murray covered up the scheme by creating false entries in the organizations general ledger and transferring less than $10,000 in each transaction to avoid triggering bank reporting requirements. Prosecutors charged Murray with using the misappropriated funds to pay personal loans and purchase luxury items. For her conduct, Murray was sentenced to 18 months in prison. A link to the DOJ’s press release can be found here. Contacts D. Jacques Smith Partner and Investigations Practice Leader Randall A. Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ Our Offices Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov Office of Public Affairs News Press Releases Justice Department Announces Compensation Process For OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture MENU News All News Blogs Photo Galleries Podcasts Press Releases Speeches Videos Archived Press Releases Archived News Press Release Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture Monday, April 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Today, the Department of Justice announced the beginning of the remission compensation process to provide recovery for victims of the international investment scheme involving OneCoin Ltd. Between 2014 and 2019, Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood, co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. (OneCoin), and others orchestrated a large, international cryptocurrency investment scheme defrauding investors from around the globe. OneCoin, which began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, marketed and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency by the same name through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. As a result of misrepresentations made about OneCoin, victims invested over $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency. The Department of Justice filed a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. Several key figures involved in the scheme have been sentenced, and the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the proceeds of the fraud scheme. More than $40 million in forfeited assets are currently available for victim compensation. Through the remission process, victims who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible for compensation. Individuals who believe they may be victims may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com . Victims may also call, email, or write to the Remission Administrator to request that a Petition Form be sent to them. The deadline for filing a petition is June 30. The Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the remission compensation process. “Victims are at the core of everything we do at the Department of Justice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. “As we did in this complex investment fraud case, the Department pursues forfeiture to take the profit out of crime and then use that money to compensate victims wherever possible. I commend the efforts of our colleagues in the Southern District of New York, our law enforcement partners, and our Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, which manages the Asset Forfeiture Program, for all of their work on behalf of the victims in this important case.” “Between 2014 and 2019, OneCoin’s founders sold a lie disguised as cryptocurrency, costing victims more than $4 billion worldwide,” said U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton for the Southern District of New York. “Today’s announcement marks an important step toward returning funds to those harmed. While no recovery can fully undo the damage, our Office will continue working to seize criminal proceeds and prioritize getting money back into the hands of victims. If you believe you may be a victim of OneCoin, you may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com.” “The victim losses accrued in this case are monumental,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr of the FBI New York Field Office. “Misled by falsified statements and empty promises, many unknowingly depleted their savings for a fraudulent investment scheme in an emerging financial ecosystem that would never pay out. With the unwavering support from the Department of Justice, the FBI maintains its commitment to returning these stolen funds to their rightful owners. Our office will continue its investigative pursuit of these criminal fraudsters — especially locating Ruja Ignatova, an FBI Top Ten Fugitive — alongside our partners at the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) and the Southern District of New York. Any information concerning this fugitive can be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov or via our tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI.” “The victims of the OneCoin scheme were misled and financially devastated by promises that were never real,” said Special Agent in Charge Jenifer L. Piovesan of IRS-CI. “Alongside our law enforcement partners, we worked tirelessly to trace illicit funds and recover them for victims. This compensation process represents a critical step toward returning stolen assets to those who were deceived. IRS-CI remains steadfast in its mission to follow the money and dismantle complex financial fraud schemes like OneCoin.” More information regarding the remission process, including eligibility criteria, updates, and frequently asked questions are available at www.onecoinremission.com or by calling 1-833-421-9748. Kroll Settlement Administration LLC is serving as the remission administrator in this matter. The FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs (OIA) provided significant assistance. The Department of Justice, through the Asset Forfeiture Program, works diligently to compensate victims of crime. Since 2000, the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), which oversees the Asset Forfeiture Program’s victim compensation program, has returned more than $12.5 billion in forfeited assets to victims of crime. MNF Attorney Advisor Drew Halter with the section’s Program Management and Training Unit is leading the remission process. Neither the Remission Administrator nor the Department of Justice will ask for any payment to participate in this remission process. Please be cautious of any individual or organization claiming to represent the Remission Administrator or the federal government in this matter. If you are a victim, any communications will come directly from the Remission Administrator or from government representatives with whom you have already had contact.
